content:
We have now completed our study of the vessels; the silver plate of the displayed ransom, the silver bowl of the deep voluntary sacrifice, and the golden spoon of the prayer and worship that rises before God like incense. Today we move forward to the animals of the dedication offerings. Each tribal leader brought five types of animal offerings, and every single one of them points to Christ.
We will look at each offering in its own time. Today we begin with the first- the young bull of the burnt offering.

Now, in the burnt offering, three animals were brought together: a young bull, a ram, and a male lamb of the first year. We will study each one separately, because each one carries its own distinct message about the nature of Christ’s sacrifice. We begin today with the young bull, because the bull is the first, the largest, and in many ways the most foundational of the three. It sets the tone for everything that follows.

In Scripture, the bull or ox is not a gentle animal. It is an animal of raw power, endurance, and labour. It pulls the plough through hard ground. It bears yokes and heavy loads mile after mile without complaint. Proverbs 14:4 says: “Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty, but from the strength of an ox comes an abundant harvest.” The ox produces the harvest through strength and service. And throughout the Old Testament, the bull was the animal of the most significant sacrifices; the animal brought by the high priest on the Day of Atonement for his own sin offering (Leviticus 16:3), the animal of the peace offering when a great covenant was being sealed. The bull was not a small animal carelessly chosen. It was the animal of weighty, costly, powerful service.

This is exactly the picture of Christ in His earthly ministry. He did not come as a distant king issuing commands from a throne. He came as a servant who worked; who laboured, who bore weight, who endured through the long years of a life given entirely in service to others. Philippians 2:7 says He “took the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men.” The word for servant here is the same word used for the most lowly, working, burden-bearing servant. Christ put on the yoke. He bent His neck to the load. He pulled the plough of human need through hard ground for thirty-three and a half years without ever setting it down.

Isaiah 53:4 gives us the content of what He bore: “Surely He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows.” The word “borne” is the word of a burden carrier,
a load-bearer, the one who takes the weight from another’s shoulders and places it on his own. The young bull of the burnt offering is this; the strong, working, enduring animal that carries what others cannot carry and does so until the work is done. And then, when the work is done, it is offered; the whole of its strength given over completely to God.

The offering was not an old bull past its working years. It was a young bull; in the full vigour of its strength, at the height of its power, not diminished and not declining. This matters greatly. Christ did not give Himself at the end of a long life after His strength had faded. He offered Himself at thirty-three years of age in the full strength of manhood, at the height of His ability. There was nothing tired or worn-out about what He gave. He gave the best. He gave the young bull.

This is the opposite of what we naturally offer. We tend to give God what is left over; the time that remains after everything else has been attended to, the energy that survives after the week’s work is done. But the young bull says: God receives the first, the full, the strongest. Proverbs 3:9 says: “Honour Yahweh with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce.”
The firstfruits are the young bull, not the old one. Christ honoured the Father with the firstfruit of His life; the young bull at full strength and He calls us to do the same.

In the burnt offering, the entire animal was consumed. There were other offerings where portions were returned to the priest, shared with the offerer, or eaten by the people. But the burnt offering was different. Everything went up. The fire consumed the whole animal; the hide, the flesh, the head, the legs, the fat, the inwards until nothing remained but ash. Every part of the bull ascended before God as smoke. Nothing was held back. Nothing was reserved for later use.

This total consumption speaks of the total surrender of Christ. John 6:38 records His own words: “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of Him who sent me.” Not some of His will. Not His will in the areas where it aligned with what He wanted. The whole will of the Father, without reservation, from the first day of His ministry to the last breath on the cross. Philippians 2:8 traces the full descent: “He humbled Himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.” Obedient to the point. Not to the edge of what was comfortable and then stopping. To the point of death. The whole animal consumed. Nothing withheld.

Hebrews 9:14 says He “offered Himself without blemish to God.” Himself. Not a substitute, not a portion, not a representative portion of Himself. The whole.
The young bull of the burnt offering is the whole Christ, given wholly, consumed entirely, ascending fully before the face of Yahweh on our behalf. This is what was placed on the altar by twelve tribal leaders, one by one, over twelve days. Twelve young bulls. Twelve complete surrenders. Twelve pictures of the one total sacrifice that would one day make all of this real.

The burnt offering was not only about what Christ gave. It is also a call to what we are to give. Romans 12:1 says: “Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.” A living sacrifice is the new covenant burnt offering. Not an animal on an altar but a life on the altar; the whole life, the strong years and the weak ones, the gifted areas and the ordinary ones, the public service and the hidden labour. The bull calls us to put the whole animal on the fire and not reach back to take something off.

This means offering our strength while it is still young; not waiting until the best years are spent on other things before finally giving God the remainder. It means offering our service without calculation; pulling the plough of holy work even when the ground is hard and the harvest is not yet visible. And it means ascending fully; not performing a partial surrender that keeps one corner of the life off the altar. The young bull was wholly consumed. Christ was wholly given. And the new creation Kohathite is called to a wholly offered life.

title: Prayer
text: Yahweh, You are the God who gave the young bull the full strength of Your Son offered wholly and without reserve on our behalf. We thank You that Christ did not offer the leftovers of a spent life but the firstfruits of a young and full strength that He bore our griefs with the shoulders of the strongest servant who ever walked this earth, and then gave every part of Himself to the fire of Your will until nothing was held back. Forgive us for the half-surrenders for the parts of our lives we have kept off the altar, for the strength we have spent on other things and then offered You what remained. Today we place the young bull on the fire. The strong years, the gifted areas, the hours of energy and health, the best of what we have; we offer it wholly to You. Let it ascend. Let nothing be held back. In Christ’s name, amen.
